children.text:
> remove the ability for penalties to be applied to the model for exhibiting undesired thought traces

This is called "the Forbidden Technique" because it just trains the model to make its thinking non-auditable. It's not helpful. You can use detection of undesired thought traces during inference as a safety breaker, but this must not feed back into training scenarios.

children.author: Majromax
children.text:
> Could a looped setup possibly remove the ability for penalties to be applied to the model for exhibiting undesired thought traces, while also reducing constraints on the space of possible solutions?

No, a looped setup does not change this configuration. A looped transformer of total length 2N (N layers, looped once)) has the same number of internal states as a standard transformer of length 2N (2N layers, not looped). In both cases, the chain of thought is only visible in the output.

The conclusion that looped transformers are uniquely dangerous requires simultaneous beliefs both that depth scaling is powerful/dangerous (reasonable, under the 'reasoning happens by the layer, not by the token' idea) and that depth scaling is easier or only possible via looping.

Could a looped setup possibly remove the ability for penalties to be applied to the model for exhibiting undesired thought traces, while also reducing constraints on the space of possible solutions? My thinking is as follows. If the CoT is visible as natural language, a loss term can be applied that discourages thoughts judged to be unethical etc. My understanding is that such regularisation, since it is unlikely orthogonal to the reward direction, can reduce model performance on the main task. I am not sure whether this is accurate in general. However, assuming that it is, looping removes the possibility of applying such feedback, contributing to better performance through lower constraints, but also inadvertently inducing undesired behaviours if they increase the expected reward.

children.text:
> The fear is that it's a slippery slope to adding more and more loops

Sure, but is it even feasible to profitably train models with "more and more added loops"? This is not quite obvious to me. The usual sort of CoT replicates patterns of human thinking that are learned in pre-training, which in a way makes it "easier" to build. And if you just stick to a handful of loops, that seems to make the high-level reasoning cleaner and more interpretable, not less so.

> If a 100T model has "equivalent performance" to a 1T model, I'd describe the 100T model as quite lousy.

You're underestimating the performance gains from CoT. On certain problems, you can push it do ridiculous results (1B LLM surpassing a 405B one):

https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2502.06703

More realistically, I believe it's around a 14x depending on the task. Thinking more deeply won't help with knowledge recall, but it does help with mathematically reasoning.

> but current proposals are for much shorter loops (just 2-fold for OP) and high-level reasoning still very much relies on CoT.

The fear is that it's a slippery slope to adding more and more loops, until CoT is replaced entirely (in theory, it could be more efficient to think in some abstract latent space than human language). Where do you draw the line? 2x loop reduce CoT length by 10%, fine, most of that CoT is junk anyway. What about a 4x loop that reduces it by 20%? Looping for a variable number of steps? You get the point.

If a 100T model has "equivalent performance" to a 1T model, I'd describe the 100T model as quite lousy. I'm not sure that's a meaningful scenario.  You may be right that CoT can be seen as a human-auditable approximation to what a looped transformer would compute with extremely deep looping, but current proposals are for much shorter loops (just 2-fold for OP) and high-level reasoning still very much relies on CoT.

I think the idea is that reducing reliance on an interpretable chain of thought is "dangerous", no matter the means. In this view, a 1T-param model that relies on an interpretable chain of thought is "safer" than a hypothetical 100T parameter model that doesn't, assuming equivalent performance. I think the reason the latter doesn't come up in discussions too much because scaling raw parameter counts to match CoT performance is currently impractical, while looped transformers (or neuralese CoT) are being actively researched and there's a feeling that there's a possibility of creating a taboo against such methods (whether that is realistic is another question).

children.author: nsingh2
children.text:
A model with N-layers is not equivalent to N/2-layers looped twice. The N/2-layer model is less general.

I think you are correct that a N-layer model would have the same or better COT controllability as a N/2-layer model looped twice. But I think the issues comes from the fact that looping allows training deeper models without it being prohibitively expensive. While if there was no looping, most would simply not train models with such effective-depth.

Either way, something like looping (more latent space thinking) was inevitable IMO.

Why would looping be overly dangerous? An n-fold looped model is entirely equivalent to a model with n times the number of params, that just happen to be shared across layers. (In fact, a bit less than that, since only a fraction of middle layers are usually looped.) If anything, it's a cheap way to explore what issues much larger models might present from a safety perspective, without these models having the in-built knowledge to actually pose that much danger (Because real-world knowledge scales with total, non-shared params).

children.author: YPCrumble
children.text:
I'm not following what a looped transformer architecture has anything to do with CoT. Are you saying that in a looped architecture less CoT is needed to come up with an answer, so it's less inspectable?

In that case, what is the difference between a model with four looped transformers, and one with additional transformers in a linear sequence, in terms of inspectability? It seems like what you are saying is that bigger/better models use fewer intermediate steps (CoT) to come up with answers so they're more dangerous...

> the raw trace was already only loosely connected to the final answer

This is not correct. In the HuggingFace incident a lot of behavior was explained very clearly by CoT.

Whether in the future, CoT will be useless because models will be able to hide their state (Astra proved to be remarkably good at this), that's definitely a possibility - but in the present, CoT is helping.

> just requires you to shift your mental model from "listening to AIs thoughts" to "monitor an engineered system for abnormal/risky states"

Interpretation and monitoring are overlapping but distinct. Monitoring detects behavior, while reading Cot can, additional, help explaining it (within the limits explained above).

People's mental model is often that the bleeding edge of X is a couple of great insights that just make things go, that are secreted away in some government or corporate lab, and that can only be found via hard to replicate feats of genius.

The reality is that moats are generally built up via soft knowledge of how to dial in massive bags of tricks, some of which might be trade secrets, some of which might be publicly known, but rarely is it a thing that people "in the know" wouldn't come up with if given sufficient budget.

Looped transformers have been an ongoing research since the beginning (universal transformers) and I think it's unlikely that z.ai was not gonna independently discover it, it being leaked was just what made it a new thing to market their "catching up" model + maybe shifted some resources earlier rather than later.

The whole interpretability/AI safety narrative is bogus rebranding of capability research (Debugging tools and improving training for what the principals, i.e. the model providers care about) and the idea that a model becomes less interpretable via Looping is humbug - the raw trace was already only loosely connected to the final answer and any monitoring at scale was using statistical associations and pattern détection which you can also do on the looped latent states, it just requires you to shift your mental model from "listening to AIs thoughts" to "monitor an engineered system for abnormal/risky states" which is what it was before already, just with anthropomorphism sprinkled on top.

Not quite the same, but I did a technical drawing where I had the model vibe code a 3D line/box tool for an illustration. The code made sure the proportions were correct, and I could orbit/zoom the camera around it to get the view I wanted. I agree, and would go even go further: procedural generation in code form is often more understandable for humans as well, and makes it easier to modify and reuse without treating it as a black box.

If I ask a model to generate an SFX sound file for the noise of falling rain for instance and it just genAI a WAV file, I don't really have any simple way to tweak it without iterating with the model itself. On the other hand if it generates a python script that procedurally generates the sound of falling rain, I have something that I can learn from and tweak myself afterwards. It's a lot less opaque and more deterministic.

Pure genAI is good for "vibecode" style development where you only monitor high-level outputs and don't care how the sausage is made, procgen is a lot better if you want to control and understand everything.

I'm sure harnesses will continue to advance, but I think training the models to do more of their thinking in code is a great thing regardless.

The silly example is writing a line of Python to count the Rs in strawberry, but people have moved on from that. I saw a video where the guy pointed out they're getting better at chess, but not great yet. If he had asked it write a chess engine (or if it had chosen to do that on its own), the model would be amazing at chess.

Lean is showing the potential for using code in the math domain. We have more trust in the compiler than we do the models. What are other non-programming areas where we could have "compilers" for the model?

Even if we restrict it to code, I'd rather the model did some trial and error experiments on the side (possibly with a sub-agent) than read pages of its thinking process where it keeps second guessing itself to make zero errors on the first try.

If I understand you correctly, I think you are incorrect.

Looped transformers allow models to do more compute in the forward pass for the same total parameter budget (e.g., required VRAM to store the model). This doesn't inherently optimize the memory bandwidth bottleneck. A simple way to see this is that if we reuse a layer during the forward pass, we still need to fetch its weights from HBM again, which incurs additional memory bandwidth usage.

The main advantage is more computation for a fixed parameter count and model-weight VRAM footprint, not more computation for a fixed HBM bandwidth budget.

children.author: gpvos
children.text: HBM memory = High Bandwidth Memory memory, i.e., generally that of a GPU chip

For those wondering what loop transformers are:

LLMs have layers of data, called weights. During inference, each layer gets computed once. Moving weights from HBM memory to the chip is a major bottleneck because to generate a token, you need to move an entire layer into the chip, compute once, move it out, move the next layer in. Hence, memory bandwidth has been the #1 bottleneck for inference.

A loop transformer optimizes this bottleneck. Instead of one layer being computed once, it will compute the same layer multiple times, increasing the model intelligence without relying memory bandwidth as much. Bandwidth is still important, but not as much anymore.

More intelligence is squeezed by using the GPU compute that is typically sitting idle during inference.

children.author: eab-

children.text: The 2x is arbitrary and in this particular case, is the fixed-point. I've seen models that do 3x loops for 3/4s of their layers. I suspect we'll see see loop counts increase as this becomes a more popular technique and may reach a point where one of the big labs is confident in their model's ability to loop "indefinitely" without becoming bogged down, reaching some logically measured point.

> This looping happens until a fixed-point is achieved (i.e another loop results in a noop).

This is not true; in the article it is made abundantly clear that it runs 2x of 28 of its layers.

A normal transformer has N layers, all of which are run forward for each token. A looped transformer is a bit different. Instead of N layers, it has K. These K layers are then looped, such that the output (not a token) of the first run of these K are fed back into the start of the K layer block. This looping happens until a fixed-point is achieved (i.e another loop results in a noop). At that point, a token is sampled. This means that tokens get different amounts of compute, depending on how challenging they are.

The thalamo-cortical loop refers to the connections in our brain between the neocortex and the thalamus, with the thalamus acting as kind of a patch panel that routes/loops activations back to different areas of the cortex.

The association cortex is that part of our cortex (brain) where activations originating from different sensory modalities come together, distinct from the sense-specific areas (visual cortex, auditory cortex, etc) where they are initially processed. This is what allows patterns/correlations across different senses to be recognized, such as lip-reading assisting with speech recognition.

I'm not aware of any transformer variants where different input modalities (text, audio, video) are processed separately, so it's all more like non-specific association cortex in that regard. There is not necessarily any advantage to initially processing different sensory inputs on their own before combining them - our brain probably just does this as a matter of plumbing - the bit of the cortex nearest to our eyes/optical nerve processes vision, etc.

The motivation for the Transformer stacked layers approach (as described by Jakob Uszkoreit whose idea it was) was linguist's sentence parse trees, where each layer of the Transformer corresponds to a layer/level of the parse tree.

The overall goal for what would become the Transformer was to create a new language modelling architecture that could take better advantage of the available parallel (GPU, etc) hardware, as opposed to RNNs which required sequential training of each time step. Uszkoreit's insight was that language is as much parallel as it is sequential, as can be seen from these parse trees where different branches (parts of the sentence) can be analyzed independently and in parallel until they join together at a higher level.

So, this is why the Transformer consists of explicitly stacked layers, because it is mimicking the layers/levels of a parse tree.

The evolution (assuming this direction sticks) of the architecture to a looped vs pass-thru design could perhaps be thought as moving away from this original linguistic inspiration to more of a brain-like architecture, although in reality the motivation is probably more practical to reduce parameter count.

What is the catch of loop transformers? Is training harder? Or what was the reason that this was not tried first? I mean first you consider a for loop and if you find a reason you unroll it. For transformers it went backwards?

children.text:
> a refreshing change from the locked-down approach of the western companies, and an interesting glimpse into the direction of SOTA LLMs

If you haven’t seen it, Thinking Machines released an interesting looped model, open weights, last week with some interesting writeups:

https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/

To be honest, I’m getting a little tired of the “eastern vs western” discourse seeping in to so much of the LLM discourse, especially when the east versus west distinction doesn’t exist as much as implied. In this case, looped model research came out of “the west” and a “western” lab was first to release an open looped model. Can we drop the whole east versus west thing and just appreciate the progress and research?

I love the transparency, or at least given technical details, that Zhipu provide - a refreshing change from the locked-down approach of the western companies, and an interesting glimpse into the direction of SOTA LLMs.

Looped Transformers are an obvious direction even if there are still problems to be worked out. The original Transformer is a bit like an unrolled for loop, and rather unnaturally pairs different sets of weights, both for attention and feed forward (knowledge) with different "layers" (aka loop iterations). Far more natural is to strive for something more like our brain's thalamo-cortical loop and association cortex, where "thought" is iterative and there are no restrictions as to what patterns/knowledge get applied when.

A similar idea has been explored before ("Universal Transformer", 2019), seemingly going nowhere, but perhaps "necessity is the mother of invention" and compute-starved Chinese companies are finding a way to make it work.

children.text: "coding" is such a terrible undersell to what these things can do. It's more like a work machine. Point it at some work, and it will go through hell and back to complete the work. Basically a meeseek. Anything it can access, it can do.

In case you're wondering what 'Generalised coding' is... it's the latest AI industry buzzword. AI companies need a label to show their models have moved past boring things like writing a python script to parse a CSV or building a todo app. Older models were mostly trained on standard swe (CRUD apps, APIs, script pipelines), rather than tools like FreeCAD, Blender or custom math stuff, and also generally couldn't 'see' that the 3D arm they coded was clipping through a wall (if they could even write the code). What's changed, and apparently requires a new label, is that a single general-purpose AI can now act like a specialist across multiple classically-math heavy domains AND visually verify its own output. That's it folks.
